description: When you are experiencing intense anxiety, a panic attack, or feel overwhelmed by fear, these strategies can help calm your nervous system and bring you back to the present moment.

strategies.name: Box Breathing
strategies.description: A structured breathing pattern used by Navy SEALs and first responders to quickly calm the nervous system. The equal-length phases create a rhythm that activates the parasympathetic response.
steps: Inhale slowly through your nose for 4 counts
Hold your breath for 4 counts
Exhale slowly through your mouth for 4 counts
Hold (lungs empty) for 4 counts
Repeat for 4-8 cycles or until you feel calmer

strategies.name: 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding
strategies.description: Engage all five senses to anchor yourself in the present moment, pulling attention away from anxious thoughts and back into your immediate environment.
steps: Name 5 things you can see
Name 4 things you can touch or feel
Name 3 things you can hear
Name 2 things you can smell
Name 1 thing you can taste
Take a deep breath and notice how you feel

strategies.name: Cold Water or Ice Technique
strategies.description: Applying cold to the face activates the mammalian dive reflex, which rapidly lowers heart rate and reduces physiological arousal. This is part of the DBT TIPP skills.
steps: Fill a bowl with cold water and ice, or grab a cold pack
Bend over and submerge your face in the cold water for 15-30 seconds, or hold the cold pack against your cheeks and forehead
Alternatively, splash very cold water on your face repeatedly
Notice the immediate shift in your heart rate and arousal level
Repeat if needed

strategies.name: Bilateral Tapping
strategies.description: Alternating left-right tapping on the body (knees, shoulders, or arms) can help reduce distress by engaging both hemispheres of the brain, similar to the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR.
steps: Cross your arms over your chest, placing each hand on the opposite shoulder (butterfly hug position)
Alternately tap your left and right shoulders at a comfortable pace
Continue for 1-3 minutes while breathing slowly
Focus on a calming image or simply notice the tapping sensation
Alternatively, tap alternately on your knees

description: When you are feeling sad, hopeless, unmotivated, or emotionally flat, these strategies can gently help shift your mood and re-engage with life. Remember: action often precedes motivation, not the other way around.

strategies.name: The 5-Minute Rule
strategies.description: When depression makes everything feel impossible, commit to doing just 5 minutes of an activity. You can stop after 5 minutes if you still want to, but most people find they continue once they start.
steps: Choose one small activity (e.g., taking a walk, tidying one surface, calling a friend)
Commit to doing it for exactly 5 minutes—no more
Set a timer on your phone
Begin the activity without judging your motivation level
When the timer goes off, check in: Do you want to continue? Either choice is okay

strategies.name: Opposite Action for Sadness
strategies.description: Depression urges withdrawal and isolation. Opposite action means gently doing the opposite—getting active and connecting with others—even when you don't feel like it.
steps: Notice the urge to withdraw, isolate, or stay in bed
Choose one small opposite action: get dressed, go outside, text a friend, or put on music
Do the activity 'all the way'—engage your body language and posture too
You don't need to feel like doing it first—act and let the feeling follow
Notice any small shifts in mood, even if they are subtle

strategies.name: Gratitude Reflection
strategies.description: Intentionally directing attention to small positives can counterbalance the negativity bias that depression strengthens. This is not about forcing positivity but gently broadening perspective.
steps: Get a notebook or open a notes app
Write down 3 things you are grateful for today—they can be very small
For each one, write a sentence about why it matters to you
Read back what you wrote and let yourself feel the appreciation
Try to do this at the same time each day to build the habit

strategies.name: Pleasant Activity Scheduling
strategies.description: Plan at least one small enjoyable or meaningful activity each day. When depressed, we stop doing the things that bring us joy, which deepens the depression.
steps: Make a list of activities that have brought you pleasure or a sense of accomplishment in the past
Choose one activity for today—pick something manageable, not overwhelming
Schedule it at a specific time (don't leave it to chance)
Do the activity as planned, regardless of your current mood
Rate your mood before and after on a 1-10 scale and notice any change
strategies.timeRequired: Varies by activity; planning takes 5-10 minutes

description: When you feel intense anger rising, these strategies can help you manage the physiological arousal and respond thoughtfully rather than reactively. Anger is a valid emotion, but how we express it matters.

strategies.name: STOP Skill
strategies.description: A DBT skill that creates a pause between the trigger and your response, preventing impulsive reactions you may regret.
steps: STOP: Freeze. Do not move, speak, or react
TAKE A STEP BACK: Physically or mentally step away from the situation. Take a breath
OBSERVE: Notice what is happening inside you (body sensations, thoughts, urges) and outside (the facts of the situation)
PROCEED MINDFULLY: Choose how to respond based on your values and goals, rather than reacting on impulse

strategies.name: Physical Release
strategies.description: Intense exercise or physical activity can metabolize the adrenaline and cortisol produced by anger, reducing physiological arousal so you can think more clearly.
steps: If possible, remove yourself from the triggering situation
Engage in vigorous physical activity: brisk walking, running, push-ups, or jumping jacks
Continue for at least 10-15 minutes
Focus on the physical sensations of exertion rather than the anger
After the intensity decreases, return to the situation with a clearer mind

strategies.name: Counting and Cooling Down
strategies.description: The classic technique of counting to 10 (or 100) gives the prefrontal cortex time to come back online after the amygdala hijack of intense anger.
steps: Pause and close your eyes if possible
Slowly count to 10 (or higher if needed), taking a deep breath with each number
With each exhale, imagine releasing some of the anger
After counting, ask yourself: What do I need right now? What would be the wisest response?
If still very activated, count again or combine with deep breathing

strategies.name: Anger Thought Challenging
strategies.description: When anger passes its initial spike, examine the thoughts fueling it. Are you making assumptions? Personalizing? Catastrophizing?
steps: Write down the thought driving the anger (e.g., 'They did that on purpose to disrespect me')
Ask: Is this thought a fact or an interpretation?
Consider alternative explanations for the other person's behavior
Ask: Will this matter in a week? A month? A year?
Develop a more balanced perspective that acknowledges your feelings without escalating them

description: When you are struggling to fall asleep or stay asleep, these strategies draw from Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I), the gold-standard treatment for insomnia.

strategies.name: Stimulus Control
strategies.description: Strengthen the association between your bed and sleep by following these rules consistently. Over time, your bed becomes a powerful cue for sleepiness.
steps: Use your bed only for sleep (and intimacy)—no phones, TV, reading, or worrying in bed
Go to bed only when you feel sleepy (not just tired)
If you cannot fall asleep within approximately 20 minutes, get up and go to another room
Do something calm and boring in dim light (e.g., read something dull, listen to soft music)
Return to bed only when you feel sleepy again
Repeat as many times as necessary
Set the same wake time every day, regardless of how much you slept
strategies.timeRequired: Ongoing nightly practice; results typically appear within 2-4 weeks

strategies.name: Progressive Muscle Relaxation for Sleep
strategies.description: A modified version of PMR designed specifically for bedtime. It releases physical tension that may be preventing sleep.
steps: Lie in bed in a comfortable position
Starting with your toes, tense each muscle group for 5 seconds, then release for 15-20 seconds
Progress slowly through feet, calves, thighs, abdomen, chest, hands, arms, shoulders, neck, and face
Focus on the contrast between tension and relaxation
After completing all muscle groups, lie still and notice the overall feeling of relaxation
Allow yourself to drift off naturally

strategies.name: Cognitive Shuffle (Serial Diverse Imagining)
strategies.description: A technique developed by cognitive scientist Luc Beaudoin that helps the mind transition from alert thinking to the random, associative thinking characteristic of the sleep onset process.
steps: Think of a random word (e.g., 'garden')
For each letter of the word, think of unrelated objects that start with that letter and briefly visualize each (G: guitar, gorilla, glass; A: apple, airplane, ant; etc.)
Move slowly through each image, spending just a few seconds on each
If you reach the end of the word, choose a new random word
The random, non-logical nature of this exercise mimics pre-sleep cognitive patterns and facilitates sleep onset

strategies.name: Sleep Hygiene Checklist
strategies.description: Environmental and behavioral factors that create conditions conducive to sleep. These are not a cure for insomnia on their own but provide a foundation for good sleep.
steps: Keep a consistent sleep and wake schedule (even on weekends)
Avoid caffeine after 2 PM and limit alcohol intake
Avoid screens (phone, tablet, TV) for 30-60 minutes before bed, or use blue light filters
Keep your bedroom cool (65-68°F / 18-20°C), dark, and quiet
Establish a relaxing pre-bed routine (warm bath, gentle stretching, reading)
Avoid clock-watching—turn clocks away from view
Get regular exercise, but not within 3 hours of bedtime
Limit naps to 20-30 minutes before 3 PM, if at all

description: When social situations feel overwhelming, these strategies can help you manage anxiety before, during, and after social interactions.

strategies.name: Pre-Event Calming
strategies.description: Before a social event, anxiety tends to build through anticipatory worry and catastrophic predictions. This strategy interrupts that cycle.
steps: Notice the anticipatory anxiety and name it: 'I'm feeling anxious about this event'
Challenge catastrophic predictions: What is the realistic worst case? How likely is it?
Remind yourself of past social experiences that went okay or well
Practice box breathing for 3-5 minutes
Set a realistic, manageable goal for the event (e.g., 'I will have one conversation' rather than 'I need to be the life of the party')
Remind yourself: you can leave if you need to

strategies.name: Focus Shift: Outward Attention
strategies.description: Social anxiety involves excessive self-focused attention (monitoring how you look, sound, or come across). Shifting focus outward reduces anxiety and improves social performance.
steps: Notice when you are focused inward on yourself (monitoring your body, replaying what you said)
Deliberately shift your attention outward to the other person or the environment
Focus on what the other person is saying rather than how you are performing
Ask the other person a question—curiosity naturally shifts attention outward
Notice details about the room, the music, or other people to ground yourself externally

strategies.name: Post-Event Processing
strategies.description: After social events, anxious individuals tend to ruminate and engage in post-mortems that magnify perceived failures. This strategy breaks that cycle.
steps: Notice if you are ruminating about the social event (replaying conversations, focusing on 'mistakes')
Remind yourself that post-event processing is a known anxiety pattern, not reality
Write down one thing that went okay or one positive interaction
Ask: If a friend described this experience, would I think it was as bad as it feels?
Engage in a distracting activity to interrupt the rumination cycle
Practice self-compassion: being imperfect in social situations is human

description: When work demands feel overwhelming, deadlines are pressing, or burnout is setting in, these strategies can help restore balance and protect your well-being.

strategies.name: Micro-Breaks
strategies.description: Short, intentional breaks throughout the workday can significantly reduce stress accumulation and improve productivity. The key is making them deliberate and restorative.
steps: Set a timer to remind yourself to take a 2-3 minute break every 60-90 minutes
During the break, stand up and stretch, look out a window, or step outside briefly
Take 5 slow, deep breaths
Do a quick body scan—where are you holding tension? Soften those areas
Return to work with renewed focus

strategies.name: Boundary Setting
strategies.description: Clear boundaries between work and personal life are essential for preventing burnout. This is especially important for remote workers.
steps: Define your working hours and communicate them to colleagues
Create a transition ritual to mark the end of the workday (e.g., a walk, changing clothes, closing your laptop in a specific way)
Turn off work notifications outside working hours
Practice saying 'I can look at that tomorrow' when contacted after hours
Schedule non-negotiable personal activities (exercise, hobbies, time with loved ones)

strategies.name: Priority Matrix
strategies.description: When everything feels equally urgent, the Eisenhower Matrix helps you distinguish between what is truly important and what merely feels urgent.
steps: List all tasks currently on your plate
Categorize each as Urgent + Important (do first), Important + Not Urgent (schedule), Urgent + Not Important (delegate or minimize), or Not Urgent + Not Important (eliminate)
Focus your energy on 'Important' tasks, whether urgent or not
Recognize that not everything that feels urgent is truly important
Communicate realistic timelines to others when needed
strategies.timeRequired: 15-20 minutes for initial sorting; brief daily check-ins

strategies.name: Values Reconnection
strategies.description: Burnout often signals a disconnection from meaning and values. Reconnecting with why your work matters (or recognizing when it doesn't) can reignite purpose or clarify needed changes.
steps: Reflect: What drew you to this work originally?
Identify the aspects of your work that still align with your values
Notice the aspects that drain you—are they changeable?
Set one small intention this week to do more of what is meaningful to you at work
If burnout is persistent, consider whether the role is still right for you—this is important information, not failure

description: Grief is a natural response to loss—of a loved one, a relationship, a job, health, or a dream. These strategies honor the grief process while supporting your well-being. There is no 'right' way or timeline for grief.

strategies.name: Dual Process Model Practice
strategies.description: Based on Stroebe and Schut's Dual Process Model, healthy grieving involves oscillating between loss-oriented activity (processing the loss) and restoration-oriented activity (attending to ongoing life tasks). Both are necessary.
steps: Recognize that it is healthy to sometimes focus on the loss and sometimes take a break from grief
Allow yourself dedicated time to grieve: look at photos, write about your feelings, cry, talk about the person or situation
Also allow yourself time to engage with daily life: work, socialize, enjoy something, plan for the future
Do not judge yourself for either mode—laughing does not mean you don't care, and crying does not mean you aren't coping
Trust the oscillation—your mind knows when to approach and when to rest

strategies.name: Continuing Bonds
strategies.description: Modern grief theory recognizes that maintaining a connection with a deceased loved one (through memory, ritual, or internal dialogue) is healthy, not pathological.
steps: Write a letter to the person you have lost, sharing what you wish you could tell them
Create or maintain rituals that honor their memory (visiting a special place, cooking their favorite meal, marking anniversaries)
Talk about the person with others who knew them—sharing stories keeps the connection alive
Consider creating a memory box or scrapbook
Allow the relationship to evolve rather than trying to 'move on' or 'get over it'

strategies.name: Self-Care During Grief
strategies.description: Grief is physically and emotionally exhausting. Basic self-care can easily fall away during intense grief, but attending to your body's needs provides a foundation for coping.
steps: Prioritize basic needs: try to eat regularly, stay hydrated, and get rest (even if sleep is difficult)
Gentle movement can help: walking, stretching, or yoga
Reduce demands on yourself where possible—it is okay to say no and to ask for help
Limit alcohol and other substances, which can intensify grief emotions
Be patient with yourself—grief takes longer than most people expect, and that is okay

description: Loneliness is the distressing feeling that comes from a perceived gap between desired and actual social connection. It is a common experience that can affect mental and physical health. These strategies help build connection gradually.

strategies.name: Small Steps to Connection
strategies.description: When loneliness has led to withdrawal, the idea of socializing can feel overwhelming. Start with the smallest possible social actions and build from there.
steps: Start with low-stakes interactions: smile at a cashier, say hello to a neighbor, chat briefly with a colleague
Send a text message to someone you haven't spoken to in a while—keep it simple ('Thinking of you, hope you're well')
Join an online community or forum related to an interest
Consider a group activity with a built-in structure (class, club, volunteer group) so socializing is easier
Set a small weekly goal: one social interaction per week, then gradually increase

strategies.name: Quality Over Quantity
strategies.description: Loneliness is not about the number of contacts but the quality of connection. Focus on deepening existing relationships rather than amassing many superficial ones.
steps: Identify 1-3 people you feel some connection with, even if it's not deep yet
Reach out to one of them with a specific invitation (coffee, walk, phone call)
During the interaction, practice being present and sharing something genuine about yourself
Ask open-ended questions and listen actively
Follow up after the interaction—consistency builds closeness

strategies.name: Self-Compassion for Loneliness
strategies.description: Loneliness often comes with shame ('Something is wrong with me'). Self-compassion counters this shame and makes it easier to reach out.
steps: Acknowledge the pain of loneliness without judgment: 'This is really hard'
Remind yourself that loneliness is a universal human experience—millions of people feel this way right now
Counter the shame narrative: loneliness says more about your circumstances than your worth
Treat yourself with the kindness you would offer a friend who is lonely
Remember that building connection takes time, and each small step counts

description: When everything feels like too much—too many demands, too many emotions, too many decisions—these strategies help you pause, prioritize, and regain a sense of control.

strategies.name: Brain Dump
strategies.description: When your mind is spinning with too many thoughts, getting everything out of your head and onto paper creates immediate psychological relief and clarity.
steps: Get a blank piece of paper (or open a notes app)
Write down EVERYTHING that is on your mind—tasks, worries, feelings, ideas—without organizing or filtering
Keep writing until your mind feels emptier (usually 5-10 minutes)
Look at the list and notice: it is finite. Your mind made it feel infinite
Circle the 1-3 things that truly need attention today
Let the rest wait—they are captured and will not be forgotten

strategies.name: One Thing at a Time
strategies.description: Overwhelm often comes from trying to hold everything in mind simultaneously. This strategy narrows your focus to one manageable step.
steps: Pause and take three deep breaths
Ask yourself: What is the ONE thing I can do right now?
Choose the smallest, most concrete action possible
Give it your full attention. When your mind tries to pull you to other tasks, gently return to this one thing
When it is done, celebrate completing it (even briefly), then choose the next one thing

strategies.name: The 3-3-3 Rule for Overwhelm
strategies.description: A simple grounding technique that combines physical movement with sensory awareness to break the cycle of overwhelm.
steps: Name 3 things you can see around you
Move 3 parts of your body (roll your shoulders, stretch your fingers, move your feet)
Name 3 sounds you can hear
This interrupts the overwhelm spiral and reconnects you with the present moment

description: Conflict is a natural part of relationships, but how we handle it determines whether it strengthens or damages the connection. These strategies help you navigate disagreements more effectively.

strategies.name: Time-Out Protocol
strategies.description: When a discussion becomes too heated, a structured time-out prevents saying things you will regret. The key is having an agreement about this BEFORE conflicts arise.
steps: When you notice you or your partner becoming too activated, say: 'I need a time-out. I care about this conversation and want to come back to it when I'm calmer.'
Agree on a specific time to return to the conversation (e.g., 'Let's talk about this in one hour')
During the time-out, engage in self-soothing: deep breathing, walking, or another calming activity
Do NOT use the time-out to build your case or rehearse arguments
Return to the conversation at the agreed time, even if it is difficult

strategies.name: Speaker-Listener Technique
strategies.description: A structured communication exercise that ensures both partners feel heard before moving to problem-solving. Each person takes turns being the speaker and the listener.
steps: The speaker holds a designated object (a pen, a pillow—anything) to indicate they have the floor
The speaker shares their perspective using 'I' statements: 'I feel... when... because...'
The listener's ONLY job is to understand—not to rebut, defend, or solve
The listener paraphrases what they heard: 'What I hear you saying is...'
The speaker confirms or clarifies until they feel understood
Switch roles. The listener now becomes the speaker
Only after both feel heard do you move to problem-solving

strategies.name: Repair Attempts
strategies.description: Based on John Gottman's research, the ability to make and receive 'repair attempts' during conflict is the strongest predictor of relationship success. Repairs are any attempt to de-escalate tension.
steps: Notice when conflict is escalating (rising voices, defensiveness, withdrawal)

Make a repair attempt: use humor ('Can we start over?'), express affection ('I love you even when we disagree'), take responsibility ('I think I'm being defensive'), or acknowledge the other person's viewpoint
If your partner makes a repair attempt, try to receive it—this is more important than the repair itself
You can create a code word or signal that means 'We're getting off track, let's reset'
Practice making repairs often—it gets easier with time
